title: Concurrency vs parallelism: interleaving vs simultaneous, IO-bound vs CPU-bound
keyPoints: Concurrency is about structure: multiple tasks making progress by interleaving, possible on a single core.
Parallelism is about execution: multiple tasks running at the exact same instant on different CPU cores.
IO-bound tasks (DB queries, HTTP calls) benefit from concurrency because threads yield the CPU while waiting.
CPU-bound tasks (encryption, sorting) benefit from parallelism because they need multiple cores computing simultaneously.
Thread count for IO-bound: cores x (1 + waitTime/computeTime). Thread count for CPU-bound: number of cores.
Use separate thread pools for IO-bound and CPU-bound work to prevent starvation.

s1_definition.oneliner: Concurrency is multiple tasks making progress by interleaving (structure, one core possible), while parallelism is multiple tasks executing at the exact same instant on different cores (execution, multi-core required).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Concurrency** – multiple tasks make progress by interleaving their execution; the OS switches between threads rapidly (time-slicing), giving the illusion of simultaneous execution; possible on a single core.
- **Parallelism** – multiple tasks execute at the exact same instant on different CPU cores; requires multi-core hardware.
- **IO-bound** – tasks that spend most time waiting for external resources (DB, network, file system); benefit from concurrency because idle threads yield the CPU.
- **CPU-bound** – tasks that spend most time computing (encryption, sorting, compression); benefit from parallelism because they need all cores busy.
- **Thread count rule** – IO-bound: `cores x (1 + waitTime/computeTime)`; CPU-bound: `cores` (or cores + 1).
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, concurrency is one teller juggling three customers. The teller serves customer-A for one minute, switches to customer-B while waiting for A's paperwork from the vault, switches to C, and back to A. All three make progress, but only one is served at any instant. Parallelism is three tellers, each serving a different customer at the same time. IO-bound work (waiting for the vault) benefits from concurrency: the teller does other work while waiting. CPU-bound work (counting cash) needs parallelism: three tellers count three piles simultaneously.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Concurrency (1 core, interleaving)
  ┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐
  │ A │ B │ C │ A │ B │ C │ A │ B │  ← time slices
  └───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘
  One core switches between A, B, C

  Parallelism (4 cores, simultaneous)
  Core 1: ████████████████  Task A
  Core 2: ████████████████  Task B
  Core 3: ████████████████  Task C
  Core 4: ████████████████  Task D
  All four execute at the same instant

  Thread Count Guidelines:
  ┌──────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
  │ IO-bound     │ cores x (1 + wait/compute)  │
  │ 4 cores,     │ 4 x (1 + 200ms/10ms) = 84  │
  │ 200ms wait   │ threads                      │
  ├──────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
  │ CPU-bound    │ cores (or cores + 1)        │
  │ 4 cores      │ 4 threads                    │
  └──────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Concurrency and parallelism are related but different concepts. Concurrency is about structure: designing your program so multiple tasks make progress by interleaving, even on a single core. Parallelism is about execution: multiple tasks running at the exact same instant on different cores.

IO-bound tasks (database queries, HTTP calls, file reads) benefit from concurrency. While one thread waits for a response, others use the CPU. Use many threads: `cores x (1 + waitTime/computeTime)`. CPU-bound tasks (encryption, sorting, compression) benefit from parallelism. They need all cores busy. Use exactly as many threads as cores. More threads just add context-switching overhead.

Never mix IO-bound and CPU-bound work in one pool. IO tasks block threads and starve CPU tasks. Use separate pools: an IO pool with many threads and a CPU pool with cores threads. At National Bank of India, the EOD batch ran on a single 4-thread pool. Database queries occupied all threads, and encryption was queued for 10 minutes. Separating into a 50-thread IO pool and a 4-thread CPU pool cut EOD time from 3 hours to 20 minutes.

Remember one sentence: IO-bound needs many threads for concurrency, CPU-bound needs cores threads for parallelism, and they belong in separate pools.
